newsitem.title: USA: USDA plans some changes to E. Coli tests.
newsitem.headline: USDA plans some changes to E. Coli tests.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department may change some procedures for E. Coli testing under its new meat and poultry inspection rule, but the implementation dates will not change, officials said Monday.

"We are very much on track to implement the E. Coli testing in January," Food Safety and Inspection Service Administrator Michael Taylor told a conference called to help government and industry prepare for the new regulation.
Meat industry representatives had said at a USDA conference earlier this month that there was some confusion over the implementation dates, especially for smaller slaughter plants.
FSIS associate administrator Tom Billy told Reuters there was no question of delaying the January 27, 1997, start date for slaughter plants to begin the E. Coli testing.
Nor would USDA delay the July 1997 date on which USDA will begin monitoring the E. Coli tests and start enforcing the E. Coli standards, Billy said.
USDA received a number of comments on procedures for E. Coli testing since the earlier conference, Taylor said.
In particular, the department would likely address several comments that E. Coli samples should be taken at only two points on a carcass, rather than three, Taylor told Reuters.
The tests for generic E. Coli are designed to measure the amount of fecal contamination on meat after slaughter.

"We are at an important juncture as we shift from the design phase of our rule to the very hard process of implementation," Taylor said at the opening Monday of the four-day National Implementation Conference.
As well as E. Coli testing, slaughter and processing establishments must implement Standard Operating Procedures by January 27 next year, according to the July 25 regulation.
Large establishments must implement Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points (HACCP) plans by January 26, 1998, while smaller ones have more time to do so.
